common_name: Dallas Blues Switchgrass (Extra-Wide-Blade Powder-Blue Native Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Dallas Blues has unusually wide, powder-blue leaf blades compared to most switchgrass cultivars, giving it a bolder, more substantial texture in the border.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Dallas Blues stands out among switchgrass cultivars for its unusually broad, powder-blue leaf blades, giving it a bolder, coarser texture than the fine-bladed straight species, topped in late summer by large, airy, pinkish flower panicles that age to a warm tan and persist through winter. Like other switchgrass cultivars it is a durable, low-maintenance native grass that tolerates heat, drought, and periodic flooding with equal ease, providing valuable structure, seed for birds, and habitat for beneficial insects. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Cloud Nine Switchgrass (Tall Airy Blue-Green Native Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass cultivars, valued for its billowy, airy flower panicles that create a soft, cloud-like effect above the blue-green foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass selections commonly grown, producing upright, blue-green foliage topped by unusually large, airy, cloud-like flower panicles in late summer that catch the light beautifully and persist as attractive tan seed heads through winter. Its height and strong vertical presence make it an excellent back-of-border screen or specimen planting, and like other switchgrass cultivars it tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, drought, and periodic flooding with ease. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump tidy and vigorous.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Variegatus requires full sun to keep its crisp white-and-green striped blades from reverting toward plain green in shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic maiden grass cultivars, producing arching, gracefully drooping blades boldly striped lengthwise in crisp white and green, creating a luminous, almost silvery effect in the garden that brightens even from a distance. In late summer it sends up tall, feathery, coppery-pink flower plumes that age to fluffy tan seed heads persisting through winter for structural interest. The large, fountain-like clump makes an excellent specimen or screen, though it needs a good amount of room to display its full arching habit; cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Nuccio's Pearl Camellia (Formal Double White-Blushed-Pink Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Pearl produces formal, perfectly symmetrical double flowers in soft white blushed with pale pink at the petal edges.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Nuccio's Pearl, from the renowned Nuccio's Nurseries camellia breeding program in California, produces exquisitely formal, tightly overlapping double flowers in soft white delicately blushed with pale pink along the petal edges, a refined color and form prized by camellia show exhibitors and collectors. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars it blooms in winter into early spring on a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen shrub with glossy, dark green foliage that provides year-round structure even when not in flower. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil, and protect from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can damage both the foliage and the delicate flowers.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Herme is a classic, long-cultivated camellia cultivar with semi-double flowers variably marbled and striped in pink, rose, and white, no two quite alike.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Herme is a long-established, historic Camellia japonica cultivar with roots tracing back to Japan, producing semi-double flowers with an irregular, ever-varying marbled pattern of soft pink, deeper rose, and white, so that individual blooms on the same shrub display a range of patterning rather than an identical, uniform color. This unpredictable variegation has made it a favorite among camellia collectors for generations. It blooms in winter into early spring on an evergreen shrub with the same glossy, dark green foliage typical of the species, and benefits from consistent moisture, acidic soil, and protection from harsh afternoon sun.
